```json
{"ranking": ["Q2", "M2", "R1"], "fault": "Q2 appears to have lost its emitter-area ratio: it is now the same size as Q1 (1:1 instead of 1:N). That leaves no ΔVBE to set the current, so the PTAT core has no well-defined operating point. The bias current is then set by channel-length modulation and start-up leakage, which makes it VDD-dependent and causes the poor line regulation."}
```

This ranking comes from reading the netlist, not from re-simulating it. Treat it as a hypothesis.

- **Why Q2 is first:** M1 and M2 have identical sizes, and so do Q1 and Q2. With nothing unequal, the loop equation reduces to I·R1 ≈ 0. A self-biased PTAT reference needs some asymmetry, and the BJT area ratio is the usual place for it. That would explain the 0.1145 V/V line regulation while vref and TC still pass.
- **Uncertainty:** the netlist format does not show BJT area or multiplicity. So I cannot confirm Q2 was originally larger; that is an inference.
- **M2 second:** the asymmetry may instead have been a width ratio on M2. I ranked it lower because M1 and M2 have the same unusual dimensions (2.559/7.483), which looks like the original design rather than a corruption.
- **R1 third:** a wrong R1 value would shift the current. I'd expect that to hurt vref and power more than line regulation, so it is the weakest candidate.

Simulating with Q2 set to a multiplicity such as m=8 should show whether line regulation recovers.
